title: As the Crow Flies Distance: Straight-Line Miles
description: Measure the straight-line distance between two places with As the Crow Flies Distance — the shortest surface path in miles and km. Free, no sign-up.
summary_sentence: For example, New York to Los Angeles is approx. 2,446 miles (3,936 km) as the crow flies — while the road journey runs hundreds of miles longer, because roads cannot follow the curve of the Earth.
quick_answer: As the Crow Flies Distance measures the shortest path between two places over the surface of the Earth, ignoring roads. Set any two places and read the straight-line distance in miles and kilometres — the honest geographic separation that road distances, flight paths and delivery zones are all measured against.

faq: Where does the phrase come from?
From the old observation that a crow flies directly, ignoring the lanes and hedgerows humans must follow. The measurement it names — the shortest surface path — is the great-circle distance.
Is this the same as the great-circle distance?
Yes. “As the crow flies” is the everyday name; great-circle is the geometric one. Both mean the shortest path over the sphere, and both are what this tool computes.
Why is the line on the map curved?
The shortest path on a sphere appears curved on most flat map projections. The curve is not a detour — it is the straight line, drawn on a map that cannot show it straight.
Can anything actually travel this distance?
Aircraft approximate it (airways permitting), signals follow it, and birds ignore the question. Everything on wheels travels further.
Exact for the spherical model between the two points chosen. The practical limit is which point in each place you pick — city centre versus suburb can differ by several miles on a long measurement.
No. Mountains, rivers and borders do not bend the surface path; they only bend the journeys humans make over it, which is the contrast the tool is for.
Crow-flies or driving distance for planning?
Both, in that order: crow-flies for the geography, driving for the logistics. A plan built on only one of them is missing half the picture.
